e.meaning: heavenly garland of flowers; royal child
e.etymology: From Hawaiian lei, a garland of flowers and by extension a beloved child, plus lani, heavenly or royal. Popular in Hawaii since the late 19th century.

assoc.t: Sweet Leilani, Bing Crosby's Oscar-winning 1937 song

e.etymology: An English pet form of Sarah, Hebrew for princess, used as a name in its own right since the 19th century.
namesakes: Sadie Robertson (Duck Dynasty star and author)

assoc.t: Sadie Hawkins dance, where girls invite the boys

e.etymology: The French form of Sophia, from Greek sophia, wisdom. In English it is used both as a pet form of Sophia and as a full name.

assoc.t: Sophie the Giraffe, classic baby teething toy
Sophie's Choice, William Styron novel and 1982 film

e.meaning: descendant of Conn, a name meaning chief
e.etymology: From the Irish surname Ó Coinn, descendant of Conn, a personal name meaning chief. A boys' name first, it has been given mostly to girls in the US since the 2010s.
namesakes: Dr. Michaela Quinn (Dr. Quinn, Medicine Woman)

e.etymology: From French Joséphine, a feminine form of Joseph, Hebrew for he will add. Napoleon's empress Joséphine made the name fashionable in English.
namesakes: Empress Joséphine (first wife of Napoleon Bonaparte)
Josephine Baker (entertainer and civil rights activist)
Jo March (Josephine, the heroine of Little Women)

e.etymology: The Slavic form of Luke, from Greek Loukas, man from Lucania in southern Italy. Its rise in the US follows NBA star Luka Dončić.

assoc.t: Luka Doncic, NBA superstar
Luka, Suzanne Vega's 1987 hit song

e.etymology: From Hebrew adam, man, related to adamah, the red earth from which Genesis says the first man was formed. It reached English through Greek and Latin.

assoc.t: Adam, the first man in the Book of Genesis

e.meaning: perhaps bright, shining one, by way of Elaine and Helen
e.etymology: A pet form of Elaine, the Old French form of Helen, from Greek Helene, often linked to a word for torch or bright light. Country singer Lainey Wilson has helped its recent rise.

assoc.t: Lainey Wilson, country music star

e.etymology: From the gemstone, whose name goes back to Latin rubinus, from ruber, red. One of the jewel names that came into fashion in the 19th century.
namesakes: Ruby Bridges (civil rights pioneer who integrated a New Orleans school at six)

assoc.t: ruby, the red gemstone and July birthstone
Ruby, a programming language
Ruby Tuesday, Rolling Stones song and restaurant chain

e.etymology: A medieval contraction of Augustine that reached England from Old French, from Latin Augustinus, a derivative of Augustus, majestic. It also became a surname, the source of the Texas capital's name.

assoc.t: capital city of Texas
Austin Powers, Mike Myers's spy spoof hero

e.etymology: From a Scottish and Northern Irish surname, James plus -son. James itself descends from the Hebrew name Jacob.

assoc.t: Jameson Irish whiskey

e.etymology: An alteration of Madeline with the -lyn ending. Madeline comes through French Madeleine from Magdalene, the woman from Magdala, a village on the Sea of Galilee.

From the biblical Garden of Eden, Hebrew eden, traditionally read as delight and perhaps borrowed from a Sumerian word for a plain. In medieval England it was also a pet form of names beginning with Ead-.

assoc.t: Garden of Eden, the biblical paradise

e.etymology: From Old French Alis, a shortening of Old High German Adalheid, built from adal, noble, and heit, kind or sort. A sister name to Adelaide, popular in England since the Middle Ages.
namesakes: Alice Walker (author of The Color Purple)

assoc.t: Lewis Carroll's heroine of Alice in Wonderland

e.etymology: From the Basque place name Xabier, from etxe berri, new house, birthplace of the 16th-century Jesuit missionary Saint Francis Xavier. His surname became a given name among Catholics.

assoc.t: Professor Charles Xavier, founder of Marvel's X-Men
Xavier University, Cincinnati school known for basketball

e.etymology: From Late Latin Dominicus, from dominus, lord. Traditionally given to boys born on Sunday, the Lord's day, and spread by Saint Dominic, the Spanish founder of the Dominican order.
namesakes: Dominic Toretto (Vin Diesel's Fast and Furious hero)
Saint Dominic (founder of the Dominican order)

e.meaning: the Titan of Greek myth who holds up the sky
e.etymology: From the Titan of Greek myth condemned to hold up the heavens; his name may come from a root meaning to bear or endure. A book of maps is called an atlas after him.

assoc.t: Titan of Greek myth who carries the sky
an atlas, a book of maps
Volkswagen Atlas SUV
Atlas Shrugged, Ayn Rand's 1957 novel

e.meaning: Christmas Day, the birthday of Christ
e.etymology: From the French form of the Late Latin saint's name Natalia, from natalis dies, the birthday of Christ. Traditionally given to girls born around Christmas.
namesakes: Natalie Portman (actress, Black Swan and Star Wars)

e.etymology: From an English surname and place name, a variant of Everleigh, usually explained as Old English eofor, wild boar, plus leah, woodland clearing. It took off for girls in the 2010s.

assoc.t: The Everly Brothers, 1950s rock and roll duo

e.etymology: The French form of Clara, from Latin clarus, clear, bright or famous. It is still the ordinary French word for clear; in English it also serves as a spelling of the older Clare.
namesakes: Claire Dunphy (the mom on Modern Family)

assoc.t: Claire's, mall jewelry and ear-piercing chain

e.meaning: uncertain; long associated with Latin miles, soldier
e.etymology: A spelling of Miles, from the Old French name Milo, of uncertain origin: perhaps Germanic, or tied to the Slavic element mil, grace or favor. It has long been associated with Latin miles, soldier.
namesakes: Myles Standish (military leader of Plymouth Colony)

e.etymology: From a Scottish and Irish surname of uncertain meaning, possibly a form of Curzon. Frontiersman Kit Carson and Tonight Show host Johnny Carson made it familiar in America.
namesakes: Johnny Carson (longtime host of The Tonight Show)

assoc.t: Johnny Carson, longtime Tonight Show host (surname)
Carson City, the capital of Nevada

e.etymology: From medieval Germanic names: either Amalric, from amal, vigor, plus rihhi, ruler, or a form of Heimrich (Henry), home ruler. Today it is usually taken from the surname and given mostly to girls.

assoc.t: emery, the abrasive mineral in emery boards

e.etymology: From Arabic amir, commander or prince, the same word as the title emir and a distant source of admiral. A separate Hebrew name Amir means treetop.
From Greek Nikolaos, from nike, victory, and laos, people. Saint Nicholas of Myra, the 4th-century bishop behind Santa Claus, made it one of the great Christian names.

assoc.t: Saint Nicholas, the bishop who inspired Santa Claus

e.etymology: A 20th-century short form of Jason, the Greek hero's name Iason, traditionally linked to the Greek verb for to heal.

assoc.t: Jace Beleren, Magic: The Gathering planeswalker

e.etymology: From the Greek name Damianos, derived from damao, to tame. Saint Damian, martyred with his brother Cosmas, is a patron saint of physicians.
namesakes: Damian Marley (reggae artist, son of Bob Marley)

assoc.t: Damian Wayne, Batman's son and a Robin

e.note: Damien, the devil child of The Omen (1976), still colors the name for some, though his is the -ien spelling.

e.etymology: A spelling of Grayson, a northern English surname meaning son of the greyve, a steward or bailiff. Many parents hear it simply as the color grey plus -son.
From an English surname and place name, Old English Cyne, a man's name meaning royal, plus leah, woodland clearing. A 21st-century favorite for American girls.
From Old French Adeline, a pet form of Adela and Adele, from Germanic adal, noble. The Normans brought it to England.

assoc.t: Sweet Adeline, the barbershop quartet standard

e.etymology: A spelling of Caden, a name American parents coined in the 1990s to rhyme with the equally fashionable Aidan, Braden, Hayden and Jayden.
From an English surname that began as a medieval pet form of the women's name Emma, from Germanic ermen, whole or universal.
namesakes: Emmett Till (teenager whose 1955 murder galvanized the civil rights movement)
Doc Emmett Brown (the inventor in Back to the Future)

assoc.t: Emmett Till, 14-year-old lynched in Mississippi in 1955
Emmett Till, teen whose 1955 lynching spurred civil rights
